stem: Which formula gives the gross profit margin?

options.content: Gross profit ÷ revenue × 100
options.rationale: Correct: gross profit as a percentage of sales.

options.content: Gross profit ÷ cost of sales × 100
options.rationale: That is the mark-up, not the margin.

options.content: Profit ÷ capital employed × 100
options.rationale: That is the return on capital employed.

options.content: Revenue ÷ gross profit × 100
options.rationale: The figures are the wrong way round.

explanation: Gross profit margin = gross profit ÷ revenue × 100.

stem: Return on capital employed (ROCE) compares profit with:

options.content: the capital employed in the business
options.rationale: Correct: ROCE = profit ÷ capital employed × 100.

options.content: the revenue of the business
options.rationale: Profit ÷ revenue gives the profit margin.

options.content: the current liabilities of the business
options.rationale: Current liabilities are used in liquidity ratios.

options.content: the cost of sales of the business
options.rationale: Cost of sales is used in gross profit.

explanation: ROCE measures the return on the long-term finance invested.

stem: A business has revenue of US\$80,000 and profit of US\$6,000. What is its profit margin?

options.rationale: This divides revenue by profit instead of profit by revenue.
This is the costs as a percentage of revenue, not the profit.
This forgets to multiply by 100.

stem: A shop's gross profit margin stayed at 35% but its profit margin fell from 12% to 8%. What is the **most** likely cause?

options.content: Its suppliers raised the prices of goods
options.rationale: That would lower the gross profit margin too.

options.content: It reduced the selling prices of its goods
options.rationale: That would lower the gross profit margin too.

options.content: It sold more goods than in the year before
options.rationale: More sales at the same margins would not cause this.

options.content: Its expenses rose faster than its revenue
options.rationale: Correct: expenses explain the gap between the two margins.

explanation: With a steady gross margin, a falling profit margin means expenses (rent, wages, etc.) have grown faster than sales.
hints: What is deducted from gross profit to give profit?

stem: Which action would **most** directly improve a business's gross profit margin?

options.content: Moving to a cheaper office to reduce rent
options.rationale: Rent is an expense; it affects the profit margin, not the gross margin.

options.content: Borrowing money to buy more delivery vehicles
options.rationale: This changes capital employed, not the gross margin.

options.content: Paying lower dividends to its shareholders this year
options.rationale: Dividends do not affect gross profit.

options.content: Buying stock from a cheaper supplier of equal quality
options.rationale: Correct: lower cost of sales raises gross profit per dollar of sales.

explanation: The gross margin depends only on revenue and cost of sales.
hints: Which costs are deducted to find gross profit?

stem: A company's ROCE is 5%. Savings accounts at banks pay interest of 7% a year (assume this rate). What does this suggest?

options.content: The company is more profitable than a bank savings account
options.rationale: 5% is lower than 7%.

options.content: The owners could earn more by saving their capital in a bank
options.rationale: Correct: the business returns less than a risk-free alternative.

options.content: The company must have a very high gross profit margin
options.rationale: ROCE does not show the gross margin.

options.content: The company has no long-term loans at all
options.rationale: ROCE does not show this.

explanation: ROCE should be compared with the return available elsewhere; here the business earns less than savings would.

stem: Why are profitability ratios more useful than profit figures alone when comparing two businesses?

options.content: They show exactly how much cash each business holds
options.rationale: Ratios of profit do not measure cash.

options.content: They predict accurately what profit will be next year
options.rationale: Ratios use past data and cannot predict accurately.

options.content: They allow for differences in the size of the businesses
options.rationale: Correct: profit is compared with sales or capital.

options.content: They include the views of customers and employees
options.rationale: Ratios ignore non-financial factors.

explanation: A large business usually makes more profit; ratios show how well each uses its sales or capital.

stem: If a business's profit rises, its profit margin must also rise.
explanation: False. If revenue rises faster than profit, the profit margin falls even though profit rose.

stem: The profit margin is always lower than or equal to the gross profit margin.
explanation: True. Profit is gross profit minus expenses, so it cannot be larger than gross profit (expenses are not negative).

stem: Match each change with the ratio it affects **first**.

left.content: A supplier raises the price of goods for resale
The business moves to premises with a higher rent
The business sells an unused building and repays a loan

right.content: Capital employed falls, so ROCE rises
Profit margin falls, gross margin unchanged

explanation: Cost of sales affects the gross margin; expenses affect the profit margin; capital employed affects ROCE.

stem: A pharmacy has revenue of US\$64,000 and gross profit of US\$22,400. Calculate its gross profit margin, to one decimal place.
A bus company made a profit of US\$13,500 on capital employed of US\$112,500. Calculate its return on capital employed, to one decimal place.
A furniture maker expects revenue of US\$95,000 next year and aims for a profit margin of 8%. Calculate the profit it is aiming for.
workedSolution:
1. Profit margin = profit ÷ revenue × 100, so profit = margin × revenue ÷ 100.
2. = 8 × 95,000 ÷ 100 = US\$7,600.

stem: Explain **two** ways a business could increase its profit margin.

points.description: Way 1, e.g. raise prices / find cheaper suppliers (1)
Explained: more profit kept from each dollar of sales; drawback e.g. customers may switch (1)
Way 2, e.g. cut expenses such as rent, energy, wages (1)
Explained: lower costs raise profit with the same revenue; drawback e.g. service quality may suffer (1)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The business could buy from a cheaper supplier, which lowers cost of sales so that more of each dollar of sales becomes profit, as long as quality does not fall. It could also cut expenses, for example by moving to cheaper premises, so profit rises even if revenue stays the same.

explanation: Raise revenue per unit or reduce costs; each method has a risk.

stem:
Sakubva Bakeries Ltd sells bread and cakes to shops in Mutare. It opened a second bakery during Year 2.

| US\$ | Year 1 | Year 2 |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Revenue | 200,000 | 240,000 |
| Gross profit | 70,000 | 72,000 |
| Profit for the year | 24,000 | 21,600 |
| Capital employed | 160,000 | 180,000 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the gross profit margin for Year 2, to one decimal place.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the profit margin for Year 2, to one decimal place.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the ROCE for Year 2, to one decimal place.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: In Year 1 the ratios were: gross profit margin 35%, profit margin 12%, ROCE 15%. Explain what the changes show.

points.description: All three ratios fell: profitability worsened despite higher revenue (1)
Gross margin fall: flour/ingredient costs rose or prices cut (1)
ROCE fall: the extra capital for the second bakery has not yet produced extra profit (1)

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: The directors say opening the second bakery was a mistake. Evaluate this view.

points.description: Evidence for: profit fell by US\$2,400 while capital employed rose by US\$20,000 (1)
Evidence against: revenue rose 20%; new bakeries take time to build sales; set-up costs in the first year (1)
Other causes: rising ingredient costs affect both bakeries (1)
Justified judgement, e.g. too early to decide; review next year (1)

explanation: Year 2: gross margin 30%, profit margin 9%, ROCE 12%: all lower than Year 1.
hints: Margins divide by revenue; ROCE divides by capital employed.

stem:
Tendai inherited money and wants to buy one of two fictional businesses in Gweru. Their latest results are shown below.

| US\$ | Hair salon | Supermarket |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Revenue | 56,000 | 420,000 |
| Gross profit | 33,600 | 105,000 |
| Profit | 12,600 | 42,000 |
| Capital employed | 63,000 | 525,000 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the ROCE of the hair salon, to one decimal place.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the ROCE of the supermarket, to one decimal place.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: The supermarket makes more profit. Explain why ROCE is a better way to compare the two businesses.

points.description: The businesses are very different sizes (1)
ROCE shows profit earned for each dollar invested (1)

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Recommend which business Tendai should buy. Justify your answer.

points.description: Salon has the higher ROCE (20% v 8%) and higher margins (1)
But salon depends on skilled staff / smaller, so profit is less certain (1)
Supermarket gives a larger total profit; the price Tendai pays matters (1)

explanation: Salon ROCE 20%; supermarket 8%. Ratios allow for size.
